column4: The section names ت ل و for reciting and following a revealed book; this verse joins proper recitation of the Book with belief, clarifying the moon's right following as a model for receiving revelation.
The section measures following by the moon's course and the Messenger's delivered word; here the Prophet says to follow him, and that following is tested by God's love and forgiveness.
The verse says messengers are sent so that they may be obeyed by God's leave (لِيُطَاعَ); it makes the right response to a sent envoy explicit against Thamud's following of their own chief.

When people demand a sign like those given to God's messengers, the verse says God knows where to place His message (رِسَالَتَهُ); the envoy's authority comes from divine choice, unlike the man who launches himself in the section.
Where Thamud reject their envoy and follow their own chief, this verse calls the revealed, blessed Book to be followed, setting the two courses against each other.
The section contrasts following the sent Messenger with following the most wretched man; this command says to follow what was sent down and not other patrons.
Noah says he conveys his Lord's messages (أُبَلِّغُكُمْ رِسَالَاتِ رَبِّي) and advises his people; this repeats the section's messenger-as-carrier and delivered-message detail.
Hud says he conveys his Lord's messages and is a trustworthy adviser; the parallel makes the section's final claim of message-delivery part of repeated prophetic speech.
Salih tells Thamud that God sent him and presents God's she-camel as a sign, opening another account of the envoy rejected in the section.

The section's elite reject the sent Salih while common followers trail their chief; here arrogant leaders ask believers whether they know Salih was sent by his Lord, making the social divide explicit.
The section sets the sent Messenger against the people who follow their wretched chief; these arrogant leaders openly say they disbelieve what the believers believe.
After the camel and its allotted drink are made a sign, Thamud hamstring it and taunt Salih to bring the threatened punishment if he is a messenger, joining rejection, speech, and action.
The earthquake that leaves Thamud fallen in their homes gives the concrete destruction behind the section's claim that the chief led his followers to ruin.
Salih says he delivered his Lord's message and advised them (بَلَّغْتُكُمْ); this directly develops the section's messenger as carrier of a message and its final word about delivery.
Shu'ayb says he conveyed his Lord's messages and advised his people; this repeats the section's specific image of a messenger handing over what he carried.
A man casts off God's signs and Satan pursues him until he becomes lost; the verse reverses the section's proper following, as one who received signs is overtaken by the wrong guide.
The same man inclines to earthly desire and follows his own whim; this specifies the mistaken course following the rejection of signs in 7:175.
Every community has a messenger, and judgment follows when the messenger comes; this repeats the section's sent-to-each-community formulation and its concern with the response.
Hud tells his people that if they turn away, he has delivered what he was sent with; this closely parallels Salih's delivered-message ending in 7:79 and the section's carrier image.
Salih is sent to Thamud and calls them to worship God; his mission gives another direct case of the divinely sent envoy set against the self-launched chief in the section.
Thamud answer Salih by recalling their hope in him and objecting to his forbidding their fathers' worship; their response supplies another direct instance of turning from the sent guide.
Salih identifies the she-camel as a sign and assigns a day of drinking to her and a day to them, giving the warning about God's camel and its drink a fuller parallel.
Thamud hamstring the camel after Salih's warning and are given three days; the act and announced consequence continue the section's camel scene.
Salih and the believers are saved from disgrace by God's mercy while the wrongdoers face the outcome; this marks the boundary between following the envoy and the destructive crowd.
A mighty cry seizes the wrongdoers at daybreak, a specific account of the ruin that follows Thamud's rejection and camel slaughter.
Thamud are left as though they had never flourished there after denying their Lord; the verse gives the finished result of the section's failed following.
The Day divides people into the wretched (شَقِيٌّ) and the happy (سَعِيدٌ); this gives the section's “most wretched” leader the lexical opposite named in its root gloss.
The wretched are assigned the Fire in this continuation of 11:105; it makes explicit the ruin that follows the section's “most wretched” course.
The Fire's lasting consequence continues the wretched person's fate in 11:106, clarifying what the section's destructive following leads toward.
The happy are placed in the Garden in contrast to the wretched of 11:105–107, giving the section's root ش ق و its stated opposite and a different end.
The Prophet calls to God with insight, “I and whoever follows me” (وَمَنِ اتَّبَعَنِي); this gives the envoy's course and its followers as the opposite of Thamud trailing their chief.
The section pairs a messenger sent with a people who deny him; this parallel says the people of al-Hijr denied the messengers.
Though clear signs came to the people of al-Hijr, they turned away from them; this supplies a further account of refusing the envoy's warning.
The punishment cry seizes the people of al-Hijr at morning, continuing the section's pattern in which rejection of the messenger ends in destruction.
What the people of al-Hijr had earned does not avail them after the blast; the verse specifies that their own course cannot shield the deniers from its end.
Those who mislead others carry their own burdens and some of the burdens of those they misled; this gives the section's leader-and-followers relation a shared moral consequence.

The section itself pairs the root ب ع ث (“send”) with ر س ل: this verse says a messenger was sent to every community to call against false gods, then distinguishes guided from doomed rejecters and says to look at the deniers' end.
The verse names Thamud's she-camel as a visible sign they wronged and connects signs with warning; it directly places the section's camel episode among God's warnings.
The section names ت ل و as reciting revealed scripture and following its trace; here the Prophet is told to recite what was revealed from his Lord's Book, sharpening that recitation-following link.
God says the Qur'an was not sent down to make the Prophet wretched; this contrasts the sent guidance with the wretched leader named in the section.
God chooses messengers from angels and people (يَصْطَفِي); the verse clarifies that the messenger is appointed, the opposite of the self-appointed chief who rises in the section.
The deniers object that the messenger is only a human like themselves and accuse him of falsehood; this repeats the contempt for following one human voiced in 54:24.
They warn that obeying a human like themselves would mean loss; the verse makes explicit the anti-human-messenger argument behind rejecting Salih.
The deniers call their messenger a man who invented a lie against God; this parallels the section's false accusation against the envoy they should follow.
Messengers are sent one after another to their peoples, who deny them and are made tales; this expands the section's sequence of sending, denial, and consequence.
The deniers object that the messenger eats food and walks in markets; this repeats the human-messenger objection that underlies Thamud's “one human” question.
They ask why an angel was not sent with the human messenger; this continues the objection to following an envoy from among themselves.
Earlier messengers are said to have eaten food and walked in markets; this answers the contempt for a human envoy voiced by the section's Thamud.
On the Day of Judgment, a follower regrets not taking a path with the Messenger; this makes the section's choice between following the envoy and another leader's path concrete.
The regretful follower calls his companion a misleader who turned him away from the Reminder, a close counterpart to people following the section's destructive chief.
The speaker says the companion made him forget the Reminder after it came; this identifies what the wrong follower's influence displaced.
The section cites this statement that Thamud denied the messengers; its root ك ذ ب and plural envoy frame are the exact rejection at the center of the image.
Salih asks Thamud whether they will not fear God, a spoken warning that parallels the Messenger's address before they answer with denial.
Salih calls himself a trustworthy messenger (رَسُولٌ أَمِينٌ); this directly joins the section's account of the sent messenger and the people who reject his word.
Salih commands the people to fear God and obey him; this is the right following that stands against their obedience to their own chief.
Salih again says to fear God and obey him, repeating the envoy's instruction at the point where the account turns to the transgressing leaders.
Salih tells them not to obey the transgressors (الْمُسْرِفِينَ); this names the wrong course that the section depicts when the people follow their most wretched man.
The transgressors spread corruption in the land and do not set things right; this specifies why the leaders whom the people follow are destructive.
Thamud answer Salih by accusing him of being bewitched, another spoken dismissal of the envoy after his warning.
They say Salih is only a human like them and demand a sign; this directly parallels their contempt for following one person in 54:24, before the camel sign is stated.
Salih assigns the she-camel a known day's drink (شِرْبٌ) and the people their day's drink, a precise parallel to the section's phrase about God's camel and its watering.
Salih forbids them to harm the camel lest the punishment seize them; this gives the warning attached to its water and the cost of rejecting it.
They hamstring the camel (فَعَقَرُوهَا), the exact deed of the section's Thamud scene.
The punishment seizes Thamud after the slaughter; this explicitly joins the action to the ruin of the followers.
The camel episode remains a sign, yet most do not believe; the verse closes this messenger-and-followers account with the same split between warning and response.
Salih is sent to Thamud, who divide into two disputing groups; this repeats the section's divinely sent messenger and shows the community splitting over him.
Nine men in the city are identified as a corrupt faction; this is the specific inner circle the section points to within the wider body of followers.
The nine swear to attack Salih and his family at night and then deny responsibility; the verse shows the chief-following faction actively plotting against the envoy.
The plotters devise a scheme while God counters it without their awareness; this reverses the self-directed plan that replaces the messenger's instruction.
The verse tells the listener to see the end of their plot and their destruction; this supplies the consequence for the corrupt inner circle named in 27:48.
Their houses lie empty because of their wrongdoing, a visible aftermath of the course the section says the chief and followers take.
God saves those who believed and feared Him from the city's destruction; this marks the distinct outcome of following rightly.
Pharaoh's people are made leaders who invite others to the Fire; this is an explicit reversal of the envoy's invitation, matching the section's destructive leader and his followers.
Those who mislead others will carry their own burdens and burdens with theirs; the verse spells out the consequences of leading followers astray.
The verse names Thamud and says Satan made their deeds seem fair and barred them from the path; this gives a specific account of the false course behind their rejection of the warning.
When told to follow what God revealed, people answer that they will follow what they found their fathers doing; this restates the contrast between revealed guidance and inherited following.
The damned wish they had obeyed God and the Messenger; this states the lost alternative to following the self-appointed leader.
They ask God to double punishment for those chiefs; the following relationship has a shared consequence, like the section's chief and his people destroyed together.
The deniers refuse to believe the Qur'an and earlier scriptures; the verse then places weak followers before the arrogant group they followed, staging the competing allegiances in the section.
The arrogant deny that they forced the weak away after revelation came; this adds the leaders' part in diverting followers from the sent word.
The weak confess that their leaders commanded them to disbelieve; the mutual blame clarifies the followers' tie to those who misled them.
A people answer their messengers, “You are only humans like us,” and call them liars; this joins the section's human-envoy objection to its accusation of falsehood.
On the Day, the followers turn to one another in accusation; this stages the afterlife reckoning of those who shared a mistaken course.
The accused answer that the followers were not believers; the verse continues the dispute between the crowd and those it followed.
The leaders deny having authority over the followers and call them transgressors; the verse identifies their shared responsibility and the followers' agency.
The word of punishment is said to have come true for both parties; this connects their bad following to its result.
The leaders admit they themselves were astray and led others astray; this states the section's destructive leadership relation directly.
The verse says both will share the punishment that day, completing the consequence of leader and followers in 37:27–32.
The rejecters are found following the tracks of their fathers, a direct case of pursuing predecessors instead of the sent warning.
They rush along those tracks (يُهْرَعُونَ), giving the section's followers-of-the-chief image a repeated form in the ancestral path they imitate.
The praised listeners hear speech and follow its best (فَيَتَّبِعُونَ أَحْسَنَهُ); this is a positive counterpart to the crowd that answers the Messenger's speech with denial.
Those who believed and feared God are saved; beside Thamud's fate, this gives the other outcome of following the warning.
If people turn away, the Messenger is not their keeper and has only to deliver clearly; this develops the section's claim that his burden is to convey, even when followers refuse.
They call the inherited religion of their fathers a community they follow; this gives the wrong-following side a second explicit ancestral formulation.
When a messenger offers better guidance, the people insist on following their fathers; this makes the rejection of a sent guide explicit.
This passage says Thamud denied the warnings; it directly names the rejection that opens the section's account of their chief and his followers.
They call him an arrogant liar (كَذَّابٌ أَشِرٌ), the counterword to the messenger's trustworthy warning in the section.
The deniers are told they will know who the liar is tomorrow; this turns their false accusation toward the consequence of rejecting the envoy.
God sends the she-camel as a trial and commands patience with them; this directly develops the sign and test implicit in the section's camel-and-drink warning.
the verse says to tell them that the water is divided between them, each receiving a turn; this is the exact scene behind the Messenger's brief “camel of God and its drink.”
They call their companion, who takes the deed upon himself and hamstrings the camel (فَتَعَاطَىٰ فَعَقَرَ); this is the section's self-appointed man acting for the crowd.
This adjacent warning names the punishment after the camel slaughter in 54:29, completing the deed-to-consequence link in the section.
The single blast destroys them like dry stalks after 54:30's warning; this gives the followers' destruction a concrete end.
The passage says Thamud and Aad denied the striking calamity; Thamud's denial repeats the section's ك ذ ب rejection before its account of the camel.
Thamud are destroyed by the overwhelming blast; the verse supplies another concise account of the fate following their denial.
The Fire is entered by the most wretched one (الْأَشْقَى), repeating the section's word for its self-starting leader in an explicit punishment setting.
The promise that whoever follows God's guidance need not fear or grieve sets a stated good outcome against the section's destructive following of the wretched leader.
When told to follow what God sent down, people insist on the path of their fathers; this is the direct reversal of following the sent message that defines the section's good track.
Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God; this sets the envoy's authority against the section's people who answer his word by following their self-appointed leader.
People refuse the call to what God sent down and to the Messenger because they rely on their fathers' practice, an explicit competing allegiance.
The Messenger is followed by those who believe and support him; this is the right human-envoy following that contrasts with the crowd who choose their own chief.
The Prophet answers a demand to change revelation by saying he follows only what is revealed; his stance is the reverse of substituting a self-chosen leader's word.
The weak followers and arrogant leaders face one another at judgment, exposing the social structure behind a crowd's choice to follow its chief.
Satan says he only invited people and they answered him, refusing their blame; this preserves the followers' responsibility even when misled.
People say they would not believe unless a human messenger were sent; the verse directly reverses the section's rejected human envoy and names the objection.
Whoever follows God's guidance is promised not to go astray or be wretched; it is the explicit opposite of following the section's most wretched leader.
The prophets are made leaders guiding by God's command; this gives the positive, divinely directed counterpart to the section's leader who carries followers to ruin.
The Prophet is told to say that obeying him is guidance; this names the right result of following the messenger whose spoken warning Thamud reject.
The prayer asks God to make its speakers leaders for the God-fearing; it presents leadership as serving right guidance, opposite the section's destructive chief.
God makes patient, certain people leaders guiding by His command; this is a specific reversal of the chief who rises on his own and leads followers astray.
The condemned say they obeyed their chiefs and great ones, who turned them from the path; this is the wrong following the section stages.
The sun cannot overtake the moon and night does not outrun day; this gives the celestial order behind 91:2 its explicit boundary and clarifies that following preserves sequence.
The command to follow what was sent down before punishment comes is the clear alternative to the Thamud who ignore their envoy's warning.
Thamud prefer blindness after guidance comes and are seized for what they earned; this is the section's wrong following and its outcome.
People choose to follow their fathers' inherited way over the messenger's invitation, another stated reversal of the section's right following.
Pharaoh misleads his people and they obey him, directly reversing the order in which the sent Messenger should be followed.
The question “shall we follow one human from among us?” (نَتَّبِعُهُ) names the refusal to follow Salih, directly opposed to following the divine envoy.
The one who denies and turns away is distinguished from the God-fearing recipient of guidance in 92:17; this is the section's choice between rejecting the envoy and following rightly.
The section's root ت ل و includes recitation and following revealed scripture; this verse speaks of people following what devils recited, a specific contrary use of following a recited account.
The Messenger's duty is only clear delivery; this is a concise formulation of the section's claim that the envoy's burden ends when he hands over the message.
The Prophet says he follows only what is revealed to him; this restates the envoy's dependence on a received message rather than a self-started course.
When asked for a sign, the Prophet says he follows only what is revealed; this repeats the section's distinction between a sent word and a man's own initiative.
The Prophet is told to follow what is revealed to him and remain patient until God judges; this is a further explicit statement of the envoy's proper course.
Earlier peoples say their messengers are only humans like them and deny their message; this extends the human-prophet rejection voiced by Thamud.

After the prior messenger rejection in 14:9, the messengers reply by asking whether there can be doubt about God, creator of the heavens and earth; this supplies their spoken counterword in that exchange.
The messengers affirm they are indeed humans like their audience, but God grants His favor; this answers the rejection of an envoy because he is human.
The Qur'an is a reminder for the one who fears, which supplies the responsive stance opposed to Thamud's rejection of the warning.
Every community has had a warner; this is a close formulation of the section's point that a messenger is sent to each people.
The moon is assigned successive phases until it returns like an old palm stalk; 36:40 then sets the sun and moon's ordered relation, completing the lunar sequence relevant to 91:2.
The deniers are driven in groups to Hell after warnings came; this echoes the section's crowd moving together to destruction after rejecting the messenger.
Those who feared their Lord are led in groups to the Garden after messengers and warning; it gives the other destination for a community's response.
The Prophet is set on a law and told to follow it rather than the desires of those without knowledge; this makes explicit the difference between received guidance and self-chosen direction.
The Prophet says he follows only what is revealed and is only a clear warner; this joins the received message to the envoy's role in the section.

The section's root ر س ل allows “messenger” for the borne word as well as its carrier; this verse calls the revelation the speech of a noble messenger (قَوْلُ رَسُولٍ كَرِيمٍ), linking message and bearer.

Like 69:40, this verse calls the revelation the speech of a noble messenger (قَوْلُ رَسُولٍ كَرِيمٍ); it concretely joins the delivered word to the one who carries it, with the messenger's identity depending on the passage's context.
This next verse says the person who avoids the reminder in 87:11 will enter the great Fire; it supplies that wretched person's consequence.
The next verse says the person there neither dies nor lives, completing the lasting consequence of the wretched person's avoidance of the reminder in 87:11–12.
The God-fearing are kept away from the Fire in contrast to the wretched of 92:15–16, clarifying the other side of the section's moral divide.
Every people is called with its imam (بِإِمَامِهِمْ), an afterlife image of a following gathered under a leader; imam can mean a leader or a record here, so the parallel remains uncertain.

In the mutual accusation begun in 37:27, one side says the other came “from the right” (عَنِ الْيَمِينِ); the phrase's force is uncertain, so this adds only the followers' dispute with those they followed.
When the leaders they followed see the punishment, they disown their followers and their former ties are severed; this gives the section's chief-and-tail relation its judgment-day reversal.
The followers wish they could return and disown those they followed, just as the leaders disowned them in 2:166; this continues the same account of following a destructive chief.
As communities enter the Fire, each curses the community before it; this extends the section's followers-and-leaders relation into a chain of groups that share the end of their course.
The people follow Pharaoh's command, and the verse says his command was not rightly guided; this directly parallels following the section's self-appointed chief over the sent messenger.
Pharaoh leads his people on the Day of Resurrection to the Fire; the verse states the destination of followers carried by their leader.
The verse says Pharaoh led his people astray and did not guide them; this is an explicit counterpart to the section's leader who takes the people after him toward ruin.
The deniers say the messenger is only a human like them and warn that obeying him would make them losers; this repeats the human-following objection voiced by Thamud.
The people tell their messenger he is a human like them and accuse him of lying; this repeats the section's linked rejection of a human envoy and false charge.
The one who follows the Reminder and fears the Most Merciful unseen is promised forgiveness and generous reward; this states the receptive response opposite Thamud's rejection.
Thamud arrogantly rebel against their Lord's command, then the thunderbolt seizes them as they look; this joins refusal of the warning to its immediate consequence.
They cannot stand up or help themselves after the thunderbolt in 51:44; this completes the destruction of the Thamud whose rejection the section depicts.
Believers are commanded to obey God and the Messenger and not turn away while hearing him; this makes the proper response to the Messenger's spoken warning explicit.

Pharaoh's people are drowned after rejecting signs, while the verse says the earlier deniers were seized for their sins (بِذُنُوبِهِمْ); this joins the section's named root ذ ن ب to followers' culpability and ruin.
The moon is darkened immediately before 75:9 joins the sun and moon; this marks the breakdown of the distinct celestial course in which the moon follows the sun.
The sun and moon are joined at the Resurrection, a boundary that reverses the separate, ordered relation pictured by the moon following the sun in 91:2.
Thamud are told to enjoy themselves for a short time before their rebellion in 51:44; this is the warning-and-delay immediately preceding the end of the same people.

The verse orders obedience to God, the Messenger, and those in authority, while disputes are referred back to God and the Messenger; it marks a boundary between delegated authority and the self-appointed chief in the section.
Those who obey God and the Messenger are promised company with the prophets and other blessed ones; this gives a positive end to following the envoy, opposite the followers' ruin in the section.
The verse commands obedience to God and the Messenger, then says the Messenger's duty is only clear delivery if people turn away; it repeats the section's message-carrier detail.
Immediately before 16:36's sending of a messenger to every community, this verse asks whether the messengers have any duty beyond clear delivery; it states the section's delivered-message claim.
The verse says earlier peoples also denied messengers and that the Messenger's duty is only clear delivery; it joins repeated rejection to the section's final delivery detail.
The verse commands obedience to God and the Messenger, then says that if people turn away, the Messenger's duty is only clear delivery; this repeats the section's carrier-and-message claim.

After the communities entering the Fire in 7:38, the earlier ones tell the later ones they have no advantage over them and both face punishment; this adds the shared consequence of the follower chain.
